title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
description: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half
body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal."Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent."It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

schema.headline: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest

title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being c
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies". In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest. Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle. "Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said. He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide". Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country. Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr. Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr. The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter. In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge

title: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans
description: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everythin
body: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong."I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off." The next day he went for a walk."[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong."It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded. For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event. At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours. "We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.The much talked about "Be Ready" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan. Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio. It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online., external They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack."It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population. However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis. "When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.  We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails. In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications". However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour. The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.The response from the government was that while  copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused."If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.It felt like an omen.

schema.headline: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans

title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Dona
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests."Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."Figure caption, Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.Figure caption, What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?Miller's hardline views sets up clash with CongressWhile Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans."Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X.  "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.Image source, Getty ImagesOn Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises."Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle

title: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
description: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since havin
body: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop."I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay. "Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral. Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

schema.headline: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour

title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
description: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in
body: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself"."Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media  meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.The actor and comedian denied the allegations. On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand. Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry. Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

schema.headline: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist

title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
description: A British stuntman and actor is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II, saying he suffered "excruciating" burns and permanent scarring in an a
body: A British stuntman and actor is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II, saying he suffered "excruciating" burns and permanent scarring in an accident while filming a scene on a burning ship.Edward Sarsfield was playing a dead soldier in the movie in 2023 when a gas line used for special effects exploded on the vessel, causing 20ft flames that made his costume catch fire, his legal claim said.He "panicked and ran" before colleagues threw bottles of water over his burns, which covered about 15% of his body, including his face, his arms and hands, he said.Sarsfield is suing August Street Films, whose defence said it admits liability for the accident, but has not made an admission about the alleged injuries or agreed to the requested £200,000 damages.Gladiator II, released in 2024, was the long-awaited sequel to the hit 2000 drama starring Russell Crowe. The follow-up was directed by Sir Ridley Scott and starred Paul Mescal and Denzel Washington.Sarsfield, 47, from Liverpool, said he was working as an extra in a scene in Morocco in which a coastal castle was under siege from an approaching ship."The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court."He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards."He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms."He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh."He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital."Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries."The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment."The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

schema.headline: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time. His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here."It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand. On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims. "As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

schema.headline: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand

title: Boy, 4, dies after Range Rover crashes on country road near Bathgate
description: A four-year-old boy has died after a car he was travelling in crashed on a country road in West Lothian.The crash involving a black Range Rover happen
body: A four-year-old boy has died after a car he was travelling in crashed on a country road in West Lothian.The crash involving a black Range Rover happened on Drumcross Road near Bathgate at about 16:30 on Friday.The boy was taken to St John's Hospital in Livingston where he died a short time later.The 28-year-old male driver of the Range Rover was taken to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary for treatment.Sgt Dave Waddell, of Police Scotland, said: "Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the boy who died at this extremely difficult time."Inquiries are ongoing and I would appeal to anyone who witnessed the crash, or has any information that may assist, to contact us, external if they have not already done so."I'd also ask drivers with dash-cams, who were in the area around the time, to review their footage for any images that could assist with our investigation."

schema.headline: Boy, 4, dies after Range Rover crashes on country road near Bathgate

title: From youth offender to junior doctor: 'I wrote a plan and stuck to it'
description: Image source, Steven BeattieImage caption, Steven Beattie was a gang member and is soon to graduate as a doctorByJennifer WilsonBBC ScotcastUpdated 1
body: Image source, Steven BeattieImage caption, Steven Beattie was a gang member and is soon to graduate as a doctorByJennifer WilsonBBC ScotcastUpdated 1 hour agoSteven Beattie spent his teenage years in and out of Polmont young offenders' institution, once described by a former governor as "the most violent prison in Scotland", external.He was sent there at 16 after drunkenly crashing a stolen car, and returned repeatedly over the next four years as his involvement with gangs and violence grew. For Steven, the turning point came when he was punished for his part in a fight by being locked up for 23 hours a day and having his TV removed."I never really had time to sit down and think where my life was going," he told the BBC's Scotcast podcast."When they took my telly, I finally had that opportunity."He asked himself - if he kept doing what he was doing, where would he be in five years' time?"If I don't like that destination, I'll have to change it," he says."I wrote out a plan and I stuck to it."Steven admits it wasn't easy for a young offender to start a new life but, after years of effort, he's about to graduate as a junior doctor.Image caption, Steven will graduate from University of Dundee Medical School in JuneSteven, who is now 37, grew up in the Hillington area of south-west Glasgow.His father had the degenerative disease Parkinson's, and his mother was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia as well as cancer, from which she later died."I was under a lot of stress at home," says Steven, who was a carer for both his parents.He left school at 15, and thinks few of his teachers understood how much stress he had been under because he had been "embarrassed" to tell them.Looking back, he gives himself "a degree of sympathy" that he didn't do so well in school because of what he was dealing with at home."A lot of the time I couldn't make school because I was up to three in the morning looking after my parents," he says.The Polmont prison riot and life as a young offenderMartin Geissler and David Cowan, Scotland home affairs correspondent, speak to Steven Beattie (pictured) about his time in a young offender institute, problems facing the prison system and his rehabilitation.Steven says avoiding gangs was "impossible" where he grew up in the 1990s and early 2000s, as "gang violence was rife".The threat of a spell in Polmont kept him out of trouble for a while, but once experienced, its deterrent effect disappeared.He made close friends while inside and, at first, life there wasn't as bad as he had feared. But he struggled to cope with the relentless noise, especially when he was trying to sleep."You've got people kicking your doors and constantly shouting and screaming, and people are in there for months and sometimes years," he says."You can imagine the effect it has on a developing brain, being in that environment for years at a time."Image source, Steven BeattieImage caption, Steven says his early life put him under a lot of stress at home Eventually, Steven made a decision to change his life and wrote down three things he had to do - leave Glasgow, quit drinking, and stop hanging around people who got into trouble.When he left Polmont, he thought most employers would find it difficult to trust him, so he started his own personal training business. He is also an award-winning MMA fighter known as 'Doctor Beatdown'.Working for himself gave him the ability to save up and move out of Glasgow. But his long-term goal was to become a doctor.He had been inspired by his dad's neurologist, who had noticed how much Steven was able to understand about his father's Parkinson's.His school grades were not enough to get him into medical school, so he attended an access course at Glasgow Kelvin college to study physiology at the University of Glasgow.That then got him into medical school, and in June, he'll graduate as a junior doctor. He hopes to specialise in either surgery, neurology or emergency medicine.Image source, Steven BeattieImage caption, Steven was in and out of Polmont over a number of yearsPolmont was back in the news last week when it emerged it had recently experienced the worst prison rioting in decades. Prison officers from four other jails were called in to restore control during the incident, which involved about 30 inmates.Linda Pollock, chief executive of the Scottish Prison Service (SPS), said it was an example of "bubbling tension" caused by increasing overcrowding.Steven says overcrowding can add to pressure inside prison."Especially in terms of rehabilitation," he says."The staff just no longer have the capacity to give attention to individual prisoners."He says a lack of attention can make inmates feel they're being left behind and unsupported.Without support they are unlikely to move on with life after prison, he says.Steven says his teenage experiences have made him more determined to enjoy the chances he has now."I think I've got an appreciation for life that a lot of people don't have because I know how bad it can get," he says.

schema.headline: From youth offender to junior doctor: 'I wrote a plan and stuck to it'

title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
description: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.The move by John Whitmire, a Demo
body: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid. "I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work. Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates."For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said. Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order. He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities." "Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change. Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration. He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , externalAbbott has also threatened to take pull  millions in funds from  cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials. The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

schema.headline: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE

title: Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players name her 'fakest celebrity fan'
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandUpdated 40 minutes agoThe New York Knicks has defended superstar Taylor Swift, after players named her as th
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandUpdated 40 minutes agoThe New York Knicks has defended superstar Taylor Swift, after players named her as the fakest celebrity fan.The basketball team's point guards Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride were asked who the least genuine celebrity Knicks fan was during a NBA 2K livestream on Thursday."At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative, cause like they just want to be seen at the game, they're not necessarily fans. Maybe Taylor Swift?" Kolek responded. McBride added: "I would agree."In May and June this year, Swift attended Game Three of the NBA Eastern Conference Finals in Cleveland and Game Four of the NBA Finals in New York City."I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolak said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Swift was part of a star-studded crowd that saw the Knicks comeback from behind to win Game Four in JuneA spokesperson for the Knicks defended Swift on Friday, telling media: "Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organisation."The BBC has approached the Knicks for comment.McBride added that "everybody else is usually solid", citing actor Ben Stiller and comedian Tracy Morgan as examples. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tyler Kolek said Taylor Swift at Knicks games was "a little performative" Kolek joked he was "gonna get some hate from the Swifties" and noted "she's got a lot going on so she can't come all the time... it's a little performative".During Game Four of the NBA Finals, Swift watched alongside musicians Este Haim, Alana Haim and actor Mariska Hargitay in matching blue shirts with either "Stevie Knicks", "Knickelback" or "Knickole Kidman" written in orange.The Knicks later went on to win their first championship in over 50 years, beating the San Antonio Spurs 94-90 in Game Five - sending New York City into a frenzy.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Miles McBride said actors Ben Stiller and Tracy Morgan were "usually solid" fansSwift has attended other games in the past, including a game between the Chicago Bulls and the Knicks in October 2014 and a match up against Orlando Magic in November 2014.The pop-star's connection with Madison Square Garden runs deep as she has performed there for two of her tours, external "Fearless" in 2009 and "Speak Now" in 2011. In July this year, Swift and her husband Travis Kelce got married at Madison Square Garden, in a star-studded ceremony officiated by actor Adam Sandler. Few details about the wedding have been released, with Swift's publicist confirming at the time both the singer and Kelce wore Christian Dior. Neither had bridesmaids or groomsmen. Swift's brother, Austin Swift, served as her man of honour, and Jason Kelce, Travis's brother, was his best man.

schema.headline: Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players name her 'fakest celebrity fan'

title: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
description: Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.The Canadian stand-up and T
body: Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentary interview with Louis Theroux that there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain."They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief."Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened."I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.Ryan continued on the podcast: "This verdict came because women were hurt, and I worry as well about what happens next."Because he's obviously spent a long time cultivating this idea that the establishment have invented these claims against him, and he's martyred himself to a growing audience who really still think that it is the courageous survivors who are the villains in this story."Ryan's comments came on the same day that former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey questioned how and why Brand was able to "get away with it so long?"Why didn't anybody intervene? Why did those around him enable him? Why didn't any of the senior executives who worked with him call time?" she said on BBC Radio 5 Live's Nick Campbell on Friday."I think they were partly mesmerised. I think he seemed to be 'cool' for a while. I think he did have charisma," added Heggessey."He brought in a young audience, which a lot of broadcasters crave. So I think all of those reasons... and as people have said, he did hide in plain sight."Bear Grylls, the adventurer and host of the Discovery Channel's show Man Vs Wild, has spoken about when he helped baptise Brand in the River Thames in 2024. "Brand's faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism," he said on X, adding that he had attended a few baptisms, including "visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes". Grylls said he attended as part of a calling of his faith "to love and serve anyone", adding it is "the sick who need healing". "Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn't want to ever discourage someone's coming to faith," he continued. But, he said, it was “right that justice has now been served."I can't imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day."Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.The actor and comedian denied the allegations.None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction."One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated."There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate."The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

schema.headline: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction

title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos
description: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the
body: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 6.5 million UK viewers in its first 28 days.The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.Filming wrapped on the three-part Christmas special at the end of August.Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming episodes, but the BBC teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" as fans eagerly await its return.The first series of The Other Bennet Sister focused on Mary, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride and Prejudice, as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England where marriage is both an aspiration and a necessity.It was mostly filmed in south Wales at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, also primarily in Wales.Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones returns to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter.

schema.headline: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos

title: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed
description: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else
body: Figure caption, Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegationsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.Image source, Married at First Sight UK, CPL ProductionsImage caption, Shona Manderson appeared on the 2023 series of Married at First Sight UKShona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard."Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part."These are real people, real emotions."Image source, Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for SXSW LondonImage caption, April Banbury took part in the 2022 series of MAFS UKOthers we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false"."I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us. "Cancelling the show does not make what happened go away," added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place."Image source, Lara EyreImage caption, Lara Eyre was a bride on the 2022 seriesOthers writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show."I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said.“Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."Where does this go from here?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Channel 4's office in central LondonAs the dust settles, there are still many questions. Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4’s review has been released, rather than the full report.We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company.Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm?We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out.In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review “did not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authorities”.The Dark Side of Married at First SightPanorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.Watch on iPlayer nowIt said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course,” then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.ukGet in touchWhat is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed
